record.paper_title: Conferences WORDS, years 1997-2017: Open Problems and Conjectures
record.original_question: Given an alphabet Σ and a pattern p, does there always exist a maximal p-free word over Σ?

evidence.quote: Given an alphabet Σ and a pattern p, a maximal p-free word over Σ exists.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let Σ be a finite alphabet and let Σ* denote the set of finite words over Σ. A pattern is a nonempty word p over a separate alphabet of variables. A word w ∈ Σ* is said to encounter the pattern p if there exists a non-erasing morphism h from the free monoid on the variables of p to Σ* such that h(p) is a factor (contiguous subword) of w; otherwise w is called p-free. A p-free word w ∈ Σ* is called maximal if no proper extension of w (by adding any letter to the left or to the right) is p-free; that is, for every a ∈ Σ, neither aw nor wa is p-free.

Prove or disprove: for every finite alphabet Σ and every pattern p, there exists a finite maximal p-free word over Σ.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not locate a published resolution of the question of whether, for every alphabet Σ and every pattern p, a maximal (i.e., non-extendable) p-free word over Σ must exist. The general area of pattern avoidance in combinatorics on words remains active, with several existence-type questions about maximal/non-extendable pattern-free words still listed among open problems. Status could not be conclusively determined.

status_evidence.title: Outstanding Challenges in Combinatorics on Words (BIRS report 12w5068)
status_evidence.snippet: Workshop report listing open problems on pattern avoidance in words, including questions on existence and structure of pattern-free words.
status_evidence.claim: Existence questions about pattern-free words remain among the active open problems in combinatorics on words.

status_evidence.title: Novel Constructions of Words with Strong Avoidance Properties
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work on constructions of words avoiding given patterns, indicating ongoing research on extendability and avoidance.
status_evidence.claim: Pattern-avoidance constructions and their extendability remain a topic of recent research.
